note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — NODDING WILDRYE SPIKE
tiles.details: Trace the central rachis of a complete mature spike: paired or clustered multiflowered spikelets attach directly at successive nodes, rather than along branches of a panicle. Canada wildrye often bends or nods and its lemma awns can spread widely, but upright or variable heads occur. Existing Bob Harms regional images show actual nodes and flowering spikes; they do not prove a Hays County rooted voucher or the Canada–Virginia species split by silhouette alone. Photo route: panels 1, 3–4 and 2 (indices 0,2,3,1) distinguish an attached regional flowering spike, fresh/mature stages and a broader nodding habit; the Bob Harms upper-culm image does not expose roots.
tiles.short: Follow a mature, often arching 8–20 cm unbranched spike with long, spreading awns.
tiles.status: GROSS PHOTO EVIDENCE — SAME-PLANT HAYS ROOTED HABIT MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · PERENNIAL BASE, TRUE LIGULE AND AURICLES
tiles.details: Follow a live plant from the perennial basal crown to the flowering culm. At the inner blade/sheath junction, spread the collar to distinguish the thin central membranous ligule from the paired clasping auricles. Bob Harms ELCA4-L depicts the collar and auricles, but the tiny free membrane edge is not separately verified for a precise arrow or millimeter measurement. Neither collar nor leaf alone separates Canada from Virginia wildrye. Photo route: panel 12 (index 11) is the actual Bob Harms collar/auricle image; panel 1 (index 0) shows only upper culm. The central free ligule edge has not been measured, and no connected Hays rooted specimen is shown.
tiles.short: Cool-season perennial; look for clasping auricles and a short membranous true ligule.
tiles.status: SOURCE PHOTO SHOWS COLLAR — OPENED 1-MM-SCALED LIGULE EDGE NEEDED

tiles.heading: 03 · ONE RACHIS NODE, MULTIPLE FLORETS
tiles.details: Magnify two or three intact mature rachis nodes at 10–20×. Each spikelet has its own outer glumes and several florets bearing separate lemmas and awns. The regional Harms J/J1 and S images teach the node and isolated spikelet; photograph the same specimen against a 1-mm ruler before disarticulating it. Hordeum little barley usually bears a three-spikelet group with mainly one floret per spikelet, not an Elymus multiflowered pair. Photo route: panels 7, 10–11 and 6 (indices 6,9,10,5) respectively show an attached rachis, detached multiflowered spikelet, disarticulation and source-identified glume-region macro. None is a 1-mm-scaled Hays voucher.
tiles.short: At each spike joint, examine the attached multiflowered spikelets rather than counting awns.
tiles.status: ATTACHMENT PHOTOS AVAILABLE — MEASURED SAME-VOUCHER NODE NEEDED

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUME BASES, LEMMAS AND AWNS
tiles.details: On two or more ripe, still-attached nodes, inspect the paired basal glumes for narrow, comparatively straight V-shaped feet. Contrast the hard pale, outward-bowed U-like glume feet often seen in Virginia wildrye; hybrids and intermediates require Elymus sp. identification. Dissect one complete multi-flowered spikelet and photograph both glumes, each lemma, palea, and the actual terminal lemma awn attachment separately. The 15–40 mm awn range is a published field-guide estimate, not a measurement from the existing JPEGs; exact glume/lemma dimensions remain unverified here. Photo route: Canada panel 6 (index 5) shows narrow glume architecture; panels 10–11 (indices 9–10) show detached reproductive parts, while Virginia panel 13 (index 12) illustrates the contrasting U-bowed glume feet. Do not call these same-voucher matched measurements.
tiles.short: Canada tends toward narrow, straighter V-like glume feet; lemma awns often about 15–40 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED AWN RANGE — MEASURED GLUME BASE AND DISSECTION MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Compare Canada and Virginia wildrye at the same maturity with two or three attached nodes and a millimeter scale. Canada generally has a looser nodding spike and narrower straighter glume bases; Virginia more often has an upright compact spike and outward-bowed hardened bases, but these are tendencies and hybrids occur. Hordeum pusillum commonly has three mostly one-flowered spikelets per node. Nassella leucotricha has a branching panicle of one-flowered spikelets with long twisted awns. Contradictory glumes and habit → Elymus sp., not a forced name. Photo route: Virginia panels 13–14 (indices 12–13) versus Canada panels 2 and 5 (indices 1,4). Check multiple mature glume bases; one Commons Canada image has an unresolved structured depicts identity discrepancy, so comparisons are not definitive vouchers.
tiles.short: Virginia wildrye has often thicker bowed glume feet; barley has spikelet triads; wintergrass has a panicle.
tiles.status: COMPARISON KEY READY — MATCHED MEASURED NODE PHOTOS NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY PHOTO AND SITE GATE
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same Hays-area authenticated rooted perennial through mature 8–20 cm spike; two or three 1-mm-scaled attached rachis nodes comparing Canada V-like glume feet with Virginia U-bowed feet; an opened short membranous true ligule distinct from auricles; one complete dissected multi-flowered spikelet with glumes, lemma, palea and awn. NEEDS_SITE_QA: inspect all existing 12 image records and comparison-panel references; retain Matt Lavin CC BY-SA credit and Bob Harms's source-specific credited scientific/educational permission (not CC); inspect original broad arrows and mobile rendering; verify public deployment separately. Retain hybrid, source-photo taxon and county-range holds until evidenced. Site-QA route: panel 12 (index 11) actual collar, panel 6 (index 5) glume macro, panel 13 (index 12) Virginia comparison, panel 10 (index 9) separated spikelet. Confirm photo identity, rights and 26 existing markers before claiming diagnostic completion.
tiles.short: 12 archived species JPEGs, 14 teaching panels and 26 markers; matched mature glume bases, local roots and measured ligule still held.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: CANADA WILDRYE (*Elymus canadensis*): follow a maturing nodding, unbranched awned SPIKE; original Harms I/i1 show green/ripe heads. In J/J1 see the central RACHIS joints carrying two or more multi-flowered units with long DIVERGING AWNS; J3 shows real exserted ANTHERS. Compare the separate detached S spikelet with original d disarticulation (true outer GLUMES versus individual inner LEMMAS/PALEAS), not just a fuzzy silhouette. Harms L shows actual clasping AURICLES and short true membranous LIGULE; these are genus clues, not the Canada-Virginia split. That split requires narrow straighter V-shaped basal glumes versus pale hardened outbowed U feet on multiple mature SAME SOURCE nodes; variable forms and documented hybrids mean contradictory specimens remain Elymus sp. Full Texas rooted crown/independent county voucher and exact measured glume-base macro still need more evidence.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Panel 3 (index 2): follow the Bob Harms actual attached flowering culm to its unbranched spike; panel 1 (index 0) shows an upper culm, not exposed roots.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Follow a live plant from the perennial basal crown to the flowering culm. At the inner blade/sheath junction, spread the collar to distinguish the thin central membranous ligule from the paired clasping auricles. Bob Harms ELCA4-L depicts the collar and auricles, but the tiny free membrane edge is not separately verified for a precise arrow or millimeter measurement. Neither collar nor leaf alone separates Canada from Virginia wildrye. Photo route: panel 12 (index 11) is the actual Bob Harms collar/auricle image; panel 1 (index 0) shows only upper culm. The central free ligule edge has not been measured, and no connected Hays rooted specimen is shown.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: On two or more ripe, still-attached nodes, inspect the paired basal glumes for narrow, comparatively straight V-shaped feet. Contrast the hard pale, outward-bowed U-like glume feet often seen in Virginia wildrye; hybrids and intermediates require Elymus sp. identification. Dissect one complete multi-flowered spikelet and photograph both glumes, each lemma, palea, and the actual terminal lemma awn attachment separately. The 15–40 mm awn range is a published field-guide estimate, not a measurement from the existing JPEGs; exact glume/lemma dimensions remain unverified here. Photo route: Canada panel 6 (index 5) shows narrow glume architecture; panels 10–11 (indices 9–10) show detached reproductive parts, while Virginia panel 13 (index 12) illustrates the contrasting U-bowed glume feet. Do not call these same-voucher matched measurements.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Versus E. virginicus: usually a more nodding, open/shaggy mature spike, longer divergent awns and glumes with straighter V-like bases. E. virginicus generally retains an erect tighter spike, shorter straighter awns and hardened outward-bowed U-like glume bases. Hybrids and variable forms occur; require several intact spikelets.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: CANADA — several mature arching/nodding spikes
panels.caption: Mature spikes arc and droop downward; the longer awns spread away from the spike axis. Look for the upper-left and mid-left bent spikes, not the unrelated plants in the background.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: CANADA — two paired spikelets and narrow glumes at a rachis node
panels.caption: Look for the central spike rachis and paired multiflowered spikelets. Long, narrow glumes flank their bases; leaflike bracts enclosing florets are lemmas. This source illustration is about GENUS architecture, not a pixel-proven V-shape glume-base measurement. Wikimedia's taxon depiction metadata is not fully consistent with the original source species label; use as source-labelled teaching reference.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: CANADA — TRUE NARROW GLUMES ON ATTACHED NODE · close original
panels.caption: Matt Lavin's CC BY-SA 2.0 photograph of a Canada wildrye flowering node; the narrow green glumes and subtended multiple-flowered spikelets are photographed directly. Compare with the separate licensed Virginia wildrye photograph showing hardened outwardly bowed glume bases. Do NOT infer millimeter dimensions or same-voucher taxonomy from these different Montana originals.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.modifications: Original RGB JPEG re-encoded without EXIF/GPS; original pixels not cropped
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: VIRGINIA — actual pale, outward-bowed bony glume bases
panels.caption: At the lowest part of the picture, each group of paired pale glumes bows away from the central point, creating a broad U or cup-shaped basal opening. The slender outer glumes flank hairy inner lemma/floret bodies. Compare Canada wildrye's typically narrower, straighter V-like glume bases, but allow intermediate hybrids.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.modifications: Original RGB JPEG re-encoded to strip EXIF/GPS
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: VIRGINIA — upright compact flowering spikes
panels.caption: Three stiffly ascending seed spikes with closely packed awned spikelets. Their posture and compactness support Virginia compared to the looser Canada mature head; photographed spikelets alone are not enough if hybridization is suspected.

memory_rule: CANADA WILDRYE: NODDING mature single SPIKE, LONG splayed AWNS, TWO OR MORE multi-FLORETED SPIKELETS per central rachis NODE, narrow STRAIGHTER basal GLUMES; tiny membranous LIGULE plus clasping AURICLES (genus clues). VIRGINIA = typically erect spike and bowed hardened U-shaped glume feet. Hybrids can overlap.
safety_note: 12 real species JPEGs plus 2 Virginia comparison panels are already present; do not recrawl those roles. Matt Lavin Commons Canada imagery includes a documented structured depicts identity discrepancy. Bob Harms educational permissions are source-specific, not CC; native-range and hybrid holds remain unchanged.
field_rule: One spike with paired multiflowered spikelets establishes Elymus-type architecture; Canada vs Virginia requires mature glume feet on multiple nodes plus habit and hybrid caution. Existing Texas anatomical photographs are real, but the same-voucher measured comparison is still missing.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
